sections.html: The red top ice blue zebra, Maylandia greshakei, is an mbuna endemic to Lake Malawi, found only around Makokola in the southeast of the lake. It inhabits the upper parts of rocky reefs next to open water, leaving the reef to feed on phytoplankton. Formerly Pseudotropheus greshakei and Metriaclima greshakei, it is still named as either of these by many sources. Aggressive and territorial, it can be combined with other mbuna but not with peaceful species such as peacocks or utaka.
Maylandia greshakei is a zebra cichlid from Lake Malawi with a bright orange dorsal fin. In the aquarium it can reach a maximum length of about 15 cm.
Collecting the fish for ornamental purposes is usually not allowed. All M. greshakei in the trade are bred ones.
Endemic to Lake Malawi. It is found only around Makokola in the southeastern part of the lake.

The fish is endemic to Lake Malawi. In the wild it is restricted to only two comparatively small areas, e.g. Crocodile Rocks and Makokola Reef, both in the southern part of the lake. This makes the species vulnerable to uncontrolled human activities.
It inhabits the upper parts of rocky reefs, usually adjacent to areas of open water, in which it leaves the reef to feed on phytoplankton.

Standard length: 135 mm SL (13.5 cm).

Aquarium base: 90 × 45 cm.

Volume: ~154 litres (90 × 45 × 38 cm).

Much of the aquarium should contain piles of rocks, arranged to form caves with small areas of open water between. A sandy substrate is best and the water should be well oxygenated. Plants should not be used as they will be eaten.

As in all cichlids from Lake Malawi, the pH should never drop below 8. In all other respects of water the fish are undemanding. Plenty of water changes are recommended to keep the fish fit and healthy, and the fish will show maximum coloration if kept this way.

It will accept most foods offered but vegetable matter in the form of spirulina flakes, blanched spinach etc. should form a large proportion of the diet. This can be supplemented with live and frozen varieties.

Correct feeding is the key to beautiful and healthy Maylandia, for fat animals become drab and sick. The balance between good, varied nutrients and fibres is crucial. Correctly fed bred fish are as beautiful as wild-collected ones.

Aggressive and territorial. It should not be kept with peace loving species, such as Peacocks or Utaka, but it can be combined with other Mbuna. The tank should be overcrowded to reduce aggression and territory formation. It is very aggressive towards others of the same species and the presence of heterospecifics helps to dissipate this. Several females should be kept per male in order to reduce harassment by the male.
Males are far more colourful than females.

Possible. Maternal mouthbrooder. It should be spawned in a species tank in a harem of one male and at least 3 females. A 120 cm aquarium is a good size and should be furnished as suggested above, along with some flat stones and areas of open substrate to act as potential spawning sites. The pH should be around 8.2-8.5 and the temperature 25–26.5°C. The fish should be conditioned with plenty of live and frozen foods. The male fish will clean and then display around his chosen spawning site, showing intense colour, and attempt to entice females to mate with him. He can be quite aggressive in his pursuits and it is in order to dissipate this aggression, that this species should be spawned in a harem. When a female is willing, she will approach the spawning site and lay her eggs there, after which she picks them up in her mouth. The male fish has egg-shaped spots on his anal fin and the female is attracted to these. When she tries to add them to the brood in her mouth she actually receives sperm from the male, thus fertilising the eggs. The female may carry the eggs for up to 3 or 4 weeks before releasing the free swimming fry. She will not eat during this period and can be easily spotted by her distended mouth. If a female is overly stressed she may spit out the brood prematurely or eat them, so care must be taken if you decide to move the fish in order to avoid fry predation. It is also worth noting that if a female is away from the colony for too long she may lose her position in the pecking order of the group. Waiting as long as possible before moving a female is recommended unless she is being harassed. Some breeders artificially strip the fry from the mother's mouth at the 2 week stage and raise them from that point as this usually results in a larger number of fry. The fry are large enough to take brine shrimp nauplii from birth.

This species was formerly classified as Pseudotropheus greshakei and Metriaclima greshakei and is still named as either of these by many sources. The genus name Maylandia is now used to describe all former members of the 'zebra' group of Pseudotropheus. An albino form of this species exists in aquaria and is occasionally available.

Maylandia greshakei is sometimes also called Metriaclima greshakei. Fish of 15 cm are never found in the natural habitat, because a wild fish does not live long enough to grow so big, and because the food in the wild is very nutrient-poor compared with almost all typical ornamental fish foods.
